docs.title: A Star Wars Military Roleplay Community on Garry's Mod
docs.text: Vision, systems design, and build plan — v1.0

docs.title: 0. The One-Paragraph Pitch
docs.text: A Star Wars military roleplay server built by someone who actually stood watch. Not a rank-cosplay server where a fifteen-year-old with a credit card outranks a squad leader who's been on the roster for a year. A server where the chain of command means something because it's load-bearing — where duties have mechanical consequence, where qualifications are earned and revocable, and where the outcome of Saturday night's operation changes what the base looks like on Sunday morning. The military texture is the product. Star Wars is the skin that makes it fun instead of grim.

docs.title: 1. Why This, and Why Most of Them Fail
docs.text:
Star Wars RP is one of the largest and most durable niches in Garry's Mod. It has been for over a decade. That's the good news and the bad news: there's a proven, self-replenishing audience, and there are also a hundred servers chasing it, most of which are dead inside four months.

They die for predictable reasons. Understanding them is the design brief.

Failure mode What it looks like Root cause Owner-as-god Founder plays the highest-ranking IC character and never loses a fight No separation between out-of-character authority and in-character authority Rank for sale Donor packages include officer commissions and battalion slots Monetizing the one thing that must stay earned Standing simulator 40 players AFK at their posts waiting for a 9pm event No gameplay loop that runs without a staff member driving it Event planner burnout One person writes every op; they quit; server dies in three weeks Content production concentrated in a single point of failure The clique Leadership is the founder's five friends; appeals go nowhere No written governance, no appeals process, no term limits Grind with no payoff Endless tryouts and promotions that unlock nothing but a new tag Progression that's cosmetic all the way down Lore lawyering Six-hour Discord arguments about whether a Phase II helmet is period-accurate No published canon scope, so everything is arguable

Every system in this document exists to close one of those holes.

The differentiator, stated plainly: the campaign layer (§7) and the sim deck (§8). Those two systems mean the server has something to do at 2pm on a Tuesday and something that matters on Saturday night. Almost nobody does both.

docs.title: 2. Setting and Canon Scope
docs.text:
Recommendation: Grand Army of the Republic, Clone Wars era, roughly 21–20 BBY.

Why this era over Imperial or First Order:

  • Clone troopers solve the identity problem. Everyone starts as an anonymous CT with a number. Individuality — a name, paint, a callsign — is something you earn. That is a genuinely powerful progression hook and it's built into the source material.
  • The unit structure is pre-built and beloved. 501st, 212th, 104th, 327th, 41st, 91st, Coruscant Guard. Players arrive already knowing what those mean and already having favorites.
  • Enemy variety without moral weight. Battle droids are guilt-free, mechanically varied, and there are excellent NPC packs for them.
  • The largest asset library on the Workshop by a wide margin. Models, maps, weapons, vehicles, sounds.

Home station: a Venator-class Star Destroyer. Not a planetary base. A ship gives you a hard, legible perimeter, a natural justification for the sim deck, a hangar that makes the flight system feel earned, and — critically — a reason the base can be boarded, which is the best passive-defense event trigger in the genre.

Published canon scope, day one. A short document that says: this is our era, these are our units, this is the Legends/canon line we're drawing, these are the deviations we've made and why. Written down, it ends 90% of lore arguments before they start. Not written down, it becomes the server's dominant social activity.

docs.title: 3. What A Player Actually Does
docs.text:
This is the section most servers skip, and it's the only one that matters. Three loops running at three timescales.

The 20-minute loop — Duty. You report to your post. Posts aren't decorative: the hangar deck has ships to service, the armory has an inventory that depletes, the bridge has sensor contacts to log, the medbay has injuries to treat, the brig has prisoners. Duty time accrues readiness for your battalion and credits for you. Randomized incident tables fire during shifts — a coolant leak, a droid infiltrator in the vents, a contact on long-range scan — so no two watches are identical.

The 2-hour loop — Training & Sim. Battalion drills, qualification courses, and the sim deck (§8). This is what fills weekday afternoons when there's no staff online.

The 1-week loop — Operations. Two to three scheduled ops per week, feeding the campaign layer. Saturday is the main event and it should feel like it.

The test for any system I add later: does it give a player something to do when there is no staff member online? If no, it doesn't ship.

docs.title: 4.1 Order of Battle
docs.text:
Launch lean. Five combat battalions, not twelve. A half-empty battalion is worse than no battalion — it demoralizes the three people in it and makes the server look dead.

Unit Identity Mechanical niche 501st Legion Line infantry, the spearhead Assault, breaching, highest headcount 212th Attack Battalion Combined arms, siege Heavy weapons, armor, demolitions 104th "Wolfpack" Search & rescue, void ops EVA, boarding actions, medevac Coruscant Guard Military police, base security Brig, ID checks, internal investigations, riot control Naval / Fleet Bridge crew and pilots Ship systems, flight ops, campaign map control Jedi Order (capped) Force users, advisory Hard cap at ~8% of roster, application-only

Add the 41st, 91st, Republic Commando, and Doom's Unit as unlock rewards tied to campaign milestones. Opening a new battalion becomes a server-wide event instead of a Discord announcement.

Jedi need a hard cap and an application gate. Every SWRP server that lets Jedi run free becomes a Jedi server with some troopers standing around. Cap it, gate it, and make Jedi mechanically support-oriented — force pushes and saber defense, not one-man army.

docs.title: 4.2 Rank Ladder
docs.text:
Two ladders, deliberately separate.

In-character (enlisted): CT → CT-Specialist → Corporal → Sergeant → Staff Sergeant → Warrant Officer In-character (commissioned): 2nd Lieutenant → 1st Lieutenant → Captain → Major → Lt. Colonel → Colonel → Commander → Marshal Commander High Command: Jedi General / Fleet Admiral — appointed, term-limited, never purchasable

Every promotion above Sergeant requires: time-in-grade, a qualification set, a sponsoring officer, and a promotion board. Promotions are logged, visible, and reversible.

Direct tie-in to your existing work: this is exactly the surface your Chain & Promotion System addon covers — Personnel File Panel, Promotion Queue, Rank Ladder Overview, overhead UI. Running the server as the live proving ground for the Chain of Command Suite is the single highest-leverage decision in this whole plan. You get a real test bed with real users, and every addon in the suite ships with "battle-tested on a live 64-slot server" as its headline. The server sells the addons; the addons make the server distinctive. Build them together.

docs.title: 4.3 Roleplay Standard
docs.text:
Set the bar at "military-plausible, not military-punishing." Real service is 90% routine and 10% chaos, and the routine is only bearable because of the people next to you. Servers that try to simulate the boring 90% faithfully die. Servers that skip it entirely feel like deathmatch with rank tags.

The compromise: - Formations are short and sharp. Ten minutes, not forty-five. A formation that runs long is a leadership failure, and it should be treated as one. - Comms discipline is enforced but taught. Publish a one-page radio brevity card. Correct people once, kindly. Enforce on the third time. - Sir/Ma'am, salutes, and reporting procedure are in effect. These cost nothing and produce enormous atmosphere. - Bearing is required in ops and formations; banter is expected everywhere else. The barracks should be loud. That's not a bug — that's the actual thing you're trying to recreate.

docs.title: 5. Progression: Qualifications, Not Rank Grind
docs.text:
Rank tells you where you sit in the chain. Qualifications tell you what you can do. Separating these is the single best structural decision available.

Qualifications are earned by passing a course, are logged to your personnel file, unlock loadout options, and can be revoked for negligence.

Qualification Gate Unlocks Basic Rifleman Boot camp Standard DC-15A/S Marksman Range course, live-fire score DC-15x, scoped optics Combat Medic Written + practical Bacta injectors, revive, triage tools Demolitions / EOD Practical course Thermal detonators, breaching charges, mine clearing Heavy Weapons Practical Z-6 rotary, RPS-6 launcher Flight — Starfighter Sim deck hours + check ride ARC-170, V-19 Flight — Transport Sim deck hours + check ride LAAT/i Armor Crew Practical AT-RT, AT-TE crew positions Comms / Sensor Ops Written Long-range scan, campaign map access Instructor Officer nomination Can certify others

Instructor is the keystone. Once players can certify other players, training scales without staff. That's how the server survives its own growth.

docs.title: 6. Progression: Credits and Cosmetics
docs.text:
Credits come from duty time, op participation, sim deck scores, and instructing. They buy:

  • Armor customization — paint, markings, kama, pauldrons, visor tints
  • Callsign registration and personalization (a real milestone for a clone)
  • Barracks bunk customization
  • Weapon skins and attachments that are sidegrades, never upgrades

Nothing that changes combat math is ever purchasable with credits or money. This is a bright line. Cross it once and the economy eats the roleplay.

docs.title: 7. The Campaign Layer (the differentiator)
docs.text:
A persistent sector map — say ten to fifteen systems in the Outer Rim — with contested control. Every operation is fought over a specific system, and the outcome persists.

How it works: - Each system has a control value that shifts based on op outcomes and, between ops, passive drift toward whoever holds the adjacent supply line. - Supply lines matter. Cut one and the connected system's defenses degrade. - Losing ground has visible consequences: the Venator's hangar has fewer functional fighters, the armory stocks fewer heavy weapons, repair times go up. Defeat is felt in the base, not just announced in Discord. - Winning a system unlocks things: new battalions, new maps in rotation, new equipment, new NPC enemy types as the Separatists escalate. - The map lives on a bridge terminal in-game and on the Discord/website, updated automatically.

Why this is worth the build cost: it converts events from disposable entertainment into a serialized story with stakes. It gives Naval and Comms a real job. It gives high command something to actually command. And it produces natural narrative arcs — "we lost Sullust three weeks ago and we're finally taking it back tonight" is a sentence that fills a server.

Build it in phases. V1 can be a Google Sheet and a hand-updated map image. Prove the loop is fun before writing a line of Lua.

docs.title: 8. The Sim Deck (the downtime solution)
docs.text:
Clone troopers train in holographic simulators. This is canon, it's flavorful, and it is a perfect lore excuse for on-demand instanced content.

A physical room on the Venator with a terminal. Any 2–8 players queue for a scenario:

  • Live-fire ranges (marksmanship qualification, scored)
  • CQB shoothouse (droid targets, timed, hostage-discrimination scoring)
  • Boarding drill (breach and clear a Separatist frigate)
  • Defense scenario (hold a position against escalating droid waves)
  • Flight sim (dogfighting and landing certification)
  • Squad tactics (objective-based, requires coordination)

Scenarios are scored, scores hit your personnel file, and top times go on a leaderboard by battalion. Sim results feed qualification progress, so the sim deck isn't a distraction from progression — it's the primary engine of it.

This is the answer to "what do I do when I log in at 3pm on a Wednesday and eleven people are online?"

docs.title: 9. Technical Build
docs.text: Caveat: the GMod addon ecosystem shifts constantly — packs get delisted, paid addons change hands, frameworks fork. Treat every specific named below as a starting point to verify at build time, not a shopping list to buy blind.

docs.title: 9.1 Framework Decision
docs.text:
Two viable paths:

Path A — Modified DarkRP. What the overwhelming majority of SWRP servers run. Enormous compatibility surface, every SWRP addon assumes it, hiring experienced developers is easy. Downside: you're fighting the framework's assumptions constantly, and it carries a lot of dead weight.

Path B — Helix or a custom base. Cleaner, more serious-RP oriented, better character persistence. Downside: far smaller addon compatibility pool, much more custom work.

Recommendation: Path A, because your addon suite is being built for the mainstream server market anyway, and dogfooding on the same stack your customers use is worth more than architectural purity.

docs.title: 9.2 Core Stack
docs.text: Layer Recommendation Notes Base gamemode Modified DarkRP Strip aggressively — no drugs, no printers, no gun dealers Admin SAM Modern, actively maintained, good logging Prop protection Falco's Prop Protection or Simple PP Non-negotiable Weapon base TFA Base Standard for Star Wars weapon packs Aircraft LFS (Luna's Flight Simulator) The genre standard for starfighters and LAATs Ground vehicles Simfphys AT-RT, AT-TE, BARC speeders Enemy NPCs VJ Base + Star Wars droid packs B1, B2, droideka, commando droids, tacticals Player models Lord Trilobite's clone packs and similar Verify current availability Bans SourceBans++ Cross-server, appealable, audit trail Rank/promotions Chain of Command Suite (in-house) Your addon — dogfood it Voice In-game 3D voice + Discord for OOC Radio addon for long-range

docs.title: 9.3 Maps
docs.text:
Primary: a good Venator map, ideally one with an interior hangar, bridge, medbay, barracks, brig, and a sim/training room. Secondary rotation for ops: rp_anaxes and similar large ground-combat maps, plus a rotating set tied to campaign systems.

Map bloat is the #1 killer of player retention on join. Every map you add lengthens the initial download. Keep the mounted collection under ~4–5 GB if you possibly can, and put the collection size on the Discord landing page honestly. A 12 GB first-join is a 60% bounce rate.

docs.title: 9.4 Hosting
docs.text:
Garry's Mod is fundamentally single-threaded. Clock speed beats core count, always.

  • Under 40 players: a good game-server host on a high-clock node. Roughly $30–60/month.
  • 40–100 players: dedicated box. Ryzen 9 or high-clock Xeon/i9, 32 GB RAM, NVMe. Roughly $80–160/month.
  • Central US location for a mostly North American audience.
  • Budget separately for a MySQL host and a small VPS for the web panel.

docs.title: 10. Administration and Governance
docs.text: This is where servers actually die, so this section is written as policy, not suggestion.

docs.title: 10.1 Two Hierarchies, Firewalled
docs.text:
Staff authority handles rule enforcement, technical issues, and player safety. Command authority handles in-character military structure.

The rules: 1. Staff rank grants zero in-character authority. A Superadmin playing a CT takes orders from a Sergeant. 2. Command rank grants zero staff powers. A Marshal Commander cannot ban anyone. 3. A person may hold both, but must declare which hat they're wearing when it matters, and may not use staff tools to resolve an in-character dispute they're party to.

Publish this in the charter. Enforce it on yourself first, publicly, the first time it comes up. That single moment sets the culture for the server's entire life.

docs.title: 10.2 Staff Structure
docs.text:
Trial Moderator (2 weeks) → Moderator → Administrator → Senior Administrator → Head of Staff → Management

  • Trial period is real. Roughly one in three should not pass, and that has to be normal and non-shameful.
  • Two-strike documented policy for staff misconduct, with the first strike public to the staff team.
  • Term limits on Head of Staff and Management — six months, renewable by review. Prevents ossification and gives people a graceful exit that isn't "quit in a rage."

docs.title: 10.3 Appeals and Evidence
docs.text:
• Every punishment requires evidence attached to the log. No evidence, no punishment. Full stop.
  • Every ban is appealable on a public-format form with a 72-hour response SLA.
  • Appeals are never reviewed by the issuing staff member.
  • An ombudsman role — one respected community member, explicitly not in the management chain, who can escalate anything directly to the owner. This is the pressure-release valve that prevents Discord coups.

docs.title: 10.4 The Founder Problem
docs.text:
The most important governance decision you will make: do not play the highest-ranking character.

Play a Sergeant. Play a medic. Play whatever you want — but not the Marshal Commander and not a General. The moment the owner is also the top of the in-character chain, every IC decision becomes unappealable, every subordinate stops giving honest feedback, and the server becomes your personal narrative rather than a shared one.

You'll get more out of it, too. The best moments in this genre come from being in a squad, not above one.

docs.title: 10.5 Documents to Write Before Launch
docs.text:
1. Server Charter — rules, punishment matrix, appeals process
  2. Canon Scope Document
  3. Standard Operating Procedures — formations, comms, engagement rules
  4. Staff Handbook — powers, escalation, evidence standards
  5. Command Handbook — promotion boards, tryout standards, discipline
  6. Qualification syllabi — one page per qualification

That's a weekend of writing. It is the highest-return weekend in the entire project.

docs.title: 11. Monetization and Legal Reality
docs.text:
Star Wars is Disney/Lucasfilm IP. You do not own it and you cannot sell it.

What this means practically: - Frame everything as donations toward server costs, never as purchases. - Sell cosmetics, queue priority, and quality-of-life only. Custom armor paint, callsign slots, extra character slots, priority join. - Never sell rank, battalion access, qualifications, or combat advantage. - No merchandise. No branded physical goods. No advertising that presents the server as an official or licensed product. - Use an established donation processor (Tebex or similar) so you're not handling payments personally. - Understand the underlying risk honestly: fan servers persist because rights holders generally tolerate non-commercial fan activity, not because they've granted permission. Keep the commercial footprint small and you stay in the tolerated zone. Get greedy and you don't.

Realistic revenue: a healthy 50-player community might see $150–400/month in donations. That covers hosting and some addon purchases. Treat it as cost recovery. If you want this to make money, the money is in your addon suite, not in the server — which is the strategic reason the two projects belong together.

docs.title: 12. Onboarding
docs.text:
You have about eight minutes to convince a new player to stay. Design accordingly.

The first fifteen minutes: 1. Auto-assigned to a recruit shuttle spawn with a clear objective marker 2. A 10-minute guided boot camp — movement, comms, salute, weapon handling, one sim deck range run 3. Assigned a sponsor: an existing player, ideally a Corporal or Sergeant, who walks them to their battalion 4. Assigned to a fire team of 3–4 within the first session 5. First qualification (Basic Rifleman) earned in session one

What kills new players: a 45-minute lecture from a bored trainer, spawning into an empty map with no direction, being told to "read the rules in Discord," and getting yelled at for something nobody explained.

The sponsor system is the highest-leverage retention mechanic available, and it costs nothing but policy. People stay for people. Give them a person in the first ten minutes. Reward sponsors with credits and count sponsorship toward promotion criteria so it actually happens.

docs.title: 13. Content Cadence
docs.text:
The rhythm is the product. Publish the weekly schedule and hold to it religiously — an unreliable schedule is worse than a sparse one.

Day Activity Mon Rest / open sim deck / tryouts Tue Battalion training (each unit runs its own) Wed Joint training or qualification courses Thu Minor operation — campaign map skirmish Fri Off-day fun event (races, deathrun, sim tournaments) Sat Main operation — the week's headline, campaign-critical Sun Debrief, promotion boards, roster maintenance

Distribute event production or it will kill you. Target six trained event planners minimum. Build a template library — a standard defense scenario, a standard boarding, a standard escort — so a planner can put together a decent op in 45 minutes instead of six hours. Rotate the Saturday op lead weekly. Nobody runs main ops two weeks straight.

docs.title: 14. Growth
docs.text:
• The Workshop collection is a marketing channel. A well-presented collection gets browsed. Cross-promote with your public Chain of Command Suite addons — every server owner who installs one sees the server.
  • Clip everything. A 40-man formation, a Venator boarding action, a LAAT insertion under fire. These are visually spectacular and short-form video is how this genre recruits now.
  • Discord server listing sites and the GMod server browser are the two biggest cold-traffic sources. Server name and thumbnail matter more than you'd think.
  • Recruit from dying servers, ethically. When a competitor collapses, forty players are looking for a home. Be visible and be welcoming. Don't poach from healthy ones — the community is small and reputation is everything.
  • Target 60–80 registered members for a healthy 25–40 concurrent. That's a real, self-sustaining server. Don't chase 128 slots.

docs.title: 15. Budget
docs.text:
Item Cost Server hosting (first 3 months) $150–350 Paid addons (weapons, models, systems, admin) $200–500 Custom development / commissioned work $0–800 Domain + web panel hosting $50–100 Discord Nitro, misc tooling $30–60 Realistic total to launch $450–1,200 Monthly steady state $60–180

You can start meaningfully lower by leaning on free Workshop content and building your own systems — which, given the Chain of Command Suite is already in progress, is a real advantage.

docs.title: 16. Phased Timeline
docs.text:
Here is the hard constraint this plan has to be built around: you ship to Cape May on September 14th. That's roughly four weeks out. Boot camp means effectively zero availability for eight weeks, and limited, unpredictable availability for a while after.

Launching a server five weeks before you disappear is the single worst thing you could do to this project. A new community without its founder present in its first weeks will either die or be captured by whoever fills the vacuum — and you will not get it back. That's not pessimism, that's just how these things go.

So the timeline is: build now, launch later.

docs.title: Phase 0 — Now through Sept 13: Paper and Assets
docs.text:
No server. No Discord announcement. No recruitment. - Write the six governing documents (§10.5). All of them. - Finalize canon scope and order of battle - Finish the Chain & Promotion System addon - Assemble and test the Workshop collection locally - Sketch the campaign map and sim deck scenarios on paper - Identify 3–5 people you'd trust as founding staff, and tell them the timeline honestly

Paper work is the ideal pre-ship task. It's asynchronous, it doesn't decay, and it's the part everyone else skips.

docs.title: Phase 1 — Post-boot camp, weeks 1–3: Stand-Up
docs.text:
• Provision hosting, build the stack, lock the collection
  • Recruit and train founding staff
  • Closed alpha with 10–15 people

docs.title: Phase 2 — Weeks 4–6: Soft Launch
docs.text:
• Open to ~30 players
  • Three battalions only: 501st, 212th, Coruscant Guard
  • Sim deck live, campaign map v1 running on a spreadsheet
  • Fix the onboarding funnel based on where people actually quit

docs.title: Phase 3 — Months 2–4: Open Launch
docs.text:
• Public listing, Workshop collection published, clip campaign
  • Add 104th and Naval
  • Campaign layer moves in-game
  • Jedi Order opens by application

docs.title: Phase 4 — Months 4+: Sustain
docs.text:
• Unlock battalions via campaign milestones
  • Establish leadership succession and term rotation
  • Premium tier of the Chain of Command Suite ships, using the server as its case study

docs.title: 17. Risk Register
docs.text: Risk Severity Mitigation Founder unavailable at a critical moment High Phase 0 timeline; deputize real authority, not figurehead titles Staff drama / community split High Written charter, ombudsman, term limits, transparent appeals Event planner burnout High Six planners minimum, template library, mandatory rotation Download size kills new-player conversion Medium Hard cap the collection, publish the size honestly Paid addon breaks after a GMod update Medium Staging server, keep a rollback snapshot, avoid abandoned addons Cheating / griefing Medium SourceBans++, prop protection, active logging, staff coverage during peak IP takedown Low Cosmetics-only monetization, no merch, small commercial footprint Server plateaus at 8 concurrent Medium Scheduled cadence, sponsor system, clip-driven recruiting

docs.title: 18. What Success Looks Like
docs.text:
Not player count. Player count is a vanity number and it lies.

Month 3: 25+ concurrent at peak. Ops running on schedule without you writing them. At least one player-run tradition you didn't invent.

Month 6: A promotion board you had no part in produces an officer you think is a good officer. Two battalions running fully independent training programs. New players being onboarded by players.

Month 12: You could take a month off and the server would be fine.

That last one is the real metric. A community that needs its founder present isn't a community — it's a project with a fanbase. The whole point of a chain of command is that it works when you're not there.

docs.title: Closing Note
docs.text:
The thing that makes military service worth recreating isn't the ranks or the uniforms or even the missions. It's that you were part of something with a shape, where your specific job mattered to people whose specific jobs mattered to you, and where the routine and the misery were shared. That's the feeling to chase. Every system in this document — the qualifications, the sponsor pairing, the campaign persistence, the firewall between staff and command — is a mechanism for manufacturing that feeling in a video game.

Get that right and the Star Wars part takes care of itself.

Standing watch.

docs.title: [SERVER NAME] — Corporal through Warrant Officer
docs.text: Role guide 2 of 4 · Drawn from the Command Handbook and Qualification Syllabi

docs.title: The job
docs.text:
You are the layer where this server actually works.

Officers set direction. Staff handle rules. NCOs handle people — training them, sponsoring them, correcting them, and noticing when someone's about to quit. Almost every member who stays does so because an NCO made them feel like they belonged in week one.

Your measure isn't your own performance in an op. It's whether your people are still here in three months.

docs.title: Leading a fire team
docs.text:
Three to five troopers. You own their training, their comms discipline, and their morale.

Weekly Do this Talk to each of them by name If someone goes a full week without being addressed directly, that's a miss Run one short drill 15 minutes of CQB or comms practice beats an hour-long lecture Know who's closest to a promotion And know the specific thing holding them back Notice absences Someone who quietly stops logging in is someone you could have kept

In an op: you are the voice your team hears. Keep your net clean, call your movements, and get your casualties to the CCP. If your medic goes down because you didn't cover them, that's on you.

docs.title: Sponsoring a new trooper
docs.text:
You'll be assigned recruits. This is the highest-leverage thing you do.

  1. Meet them in their first session. Not later. Now.
  2. Walk them to their battalion physically. Don't link them a channel.
  3. Introduce them to their fire team by name.
  4. Check in after their second session. This is the one everyone skips and it's the one that matters.
  5. Push them toward their second qualification within two weeks.

Sponsorship counts toward your own promotion, and five sponsored recruits reaching Specialist earns the Sponsor Ribbon. That's deliberate — we pay for this work because it's the work that keeps the server alive.

docs.title: Running a tryout
docs.text:
Rule Standard Duration 30 minutes maximum Notice 24 hours minimum, announced publicly Minimum attendance One. Never cancel on a single candidate — they made time for you Rubric Published before the tryout. They should know exactly what's measured Result Same session, in writing Retry 7 days. No lifetime bars, ever

Standard structure: bearing (5) → knowledge check (5) → marksmanship (5) → practical scenario (10) → interview (5).

docs.title: Absolutely prohibited
docs.text:
• Hazing. Any form. Not tradition, not character-building, not "how it was done for me." This is a command discipline matter and probably a Charter violation.
  • Endurance filtering. Standing people at attention for 40 minutes measures patience, not aptitude, and selects for exactly the wrong people.
  • Vague failure. "Not ready" is not feedback. Tell them the specific thing and the date they can retry.

docs.title: Certifying (Instructor qualification)
docs.text:
You can only certify in qualifications you personally hold.

The method — all four phases, every time:

Explain → Demonstrate → Practice → Assess

Lecture alone doesn't work. If you're talking for more than a third of the course, restructure it.

docs.title: The instructor code
docs.text:
1. You are not the point. The student is.
  2. Score the published standard, not your personal preference.
  3. Never fail someone without telling them exactly how to pass.
  4. No hazing. Ever. Any form. Any reason.
  5. Stay under the time limit — every time you run long, your next class is smaller.
  6. If everyone fails, the course is broken, not the students.
  7. Recognize the biggest improvement, not just the highest score.

Log every certification: candidate, qual, date, instructor, score by block, pass/defer/fail, written feedback.

Stay current: one course per month minimum. Student feedback is collected anonymously and reviewed.

docs.title: Correcting people
docs.text:
Praise publicly. Correct privately. Always. No exceptions.

Step When Verbal counseling First time. Private conversation, noted in the file. Written counseling Pattern. Documented, signed, includes a specific improvement plan and a date. Escalate to your officer Beyond that — extra duty, qual suspension, and rank reduction aren't yours to issue

docs.title: Hard rules
docs.text:
• No mass punishment. Punishing a squad for one person's mistake is banned. It builds resentment and drives people off the server.
  • Never correct while angry. Wait a session. Nothing is that urgent.
  • "Do better" is not counseling. Name the behavior, name the fix.
  • Rule violations go to staff, not you. Cheating, harassment, RDM — report it. You handle performance; staff handle rules. Don't blur that line.

docs.title: The firewall
docs.text:
If you also hold a staff position: your staff rank gives you zero additional in-character authority, and your NCO rank gives you zero moderation authority.

When it matters, say which hat you're wearing out loud. And never use staff tools in a dispute you're personally part of — call another staff member. Every time.

docs.title: Your weekly checklist
docs.text:
1. Did I correct anyone publicly this week? (Don't.)
  2. Did anyone on my team go a week without me speaking to them by name?
  3. Who's closest to a promotion, and what specifically is in the way?
  4. Did I run at least one drill?
  5. Have I checked on my sponsored recruits?
  6. Did anyone leave, and do I know why?
  7. Am I still enjoying this? If no, take an LOA before you burn out and take three people with you.

docs.title: Welcome aboard
docs.text:
You're a clone trooper in the Grand Army of the Republic, stationed aboard the RSD [SHIP NAME]. You have a number, not a name — yet. You'll get one.

Nobody expects you to know anything. The only thing you can do wrong in your first session is stay quiet when you're confused.

docs.title: What happens in your first fifteen minutes
docs.text:
Step What 1. Spawn You arrive on a recruit shuttle. Follow the marker. 2. Boot camp 10 minutes. Movement, weapons, comms, one range run. 3. Basic Rifleman You earn your first qualification here. Nobody fails this course — if you struggle, the instructor works with you until you pass. 4. Your sponsor An NCO gets assigned to you. They walk you to your battalion. Ask them everything. That's the job. 5. Your fire team You're placed in a team of 3–4. These are your people.

If nobody has assigned you a sponsor within your first session, ask for one. It's supposed to happen automatically and it's a failure on our end if it doesn't.

docs.title: The five things to learn first
docs.text:
1. The radio format.

"[Them], this is [me], [message], over."

2. Three calls that stop everything. CHECK FIRE · MAN DOWN · CONTACT

3. Weapons Cold is the base default. Holstered. Don't walk around the ship with a rifle out.

4. "Sir" or "Ma'am" to officers, rank to NCOs. Reporting sounds like: "Sir, CT-2247 reporting as ordered."

5. Bearing is situational. Formations, ops, posts, and the bridge — discipline. Barracks and mess — be as loud as you want. Knowing which room you're in is the whole skill.

docs.title: Your first three goals
docs.text:
Goal How Earn a name Complete Basic Rifleman + 10 hours duty time, or do something memorable in an op. Your squad usually names you, and it's usually about something embarrassing. That's tradition. Pick up a second qualification Combat Medic and Comms are the easiest to get and the most useful to a squad. Marksman is the most fun. Make Specialist, then Corporal Specialist is 10 hours and 2 quals. Corporal is 20 hours, 3 quals, and your sponsor putting your name forward.

Rank and qualifications are different things. Rank is where you sit in the chain. Quals are what you're allowed to do. A Corporal with EOD can do things a Captain without it can't. Chase quals.

docs.title: Things that will trip you up
docs.text:
• Don't carry gear you're not qualified for. Picking up a sniper rifle without Marksman is an armory violation, not a shortcut.
  • Don't shoot friendlies. It happens once and it's an accident. Twice in a session and someone will have a conversation with you.
  • Don't break an event to complain. Note it, raise it after.
  • Don't argue in a staff sit. Say your piece once, then appeal if you disagree. Arguing has never once worked.
  • Don't lore-argue. If you think something's wrong, file a ruling request. Do not start a thread.

docs.title: Speak up
docs.text:
If an order seems wrong, say so before you execute it, then execute it.

"Sir, recommend we approach from the east instead — request permission to advise."

That is not insubordination and you will not be punished for it. An officer who punishes you for that is the one out of line, and you should report it. Silence during a bad plan is how operations fail.

Three things are never insubordination: refusing an order that breaks the Charter, asking a clarifying question, and raising a concern before you act.

docs.title: When something goes wrong
docs.text:
Problem Where it goes Someone's cheating, harassing, or breaking rules Staff — report it, don't handle it yourself An order was unfair, or a leader treated you badly Your chain of command — start with your NCO Your chain of command is the problem The Ombudsman — that's exactly what the role is for You got punished and it was wrong File an appeal. 72-hour response. If there's no evidence in the log, you win automatically.

You will not be retaliated against for reporting or appealing. That's a removable offense for staff.

docs.title: Life happens
docs.text:
Leave of absence is free, unlimited, and requires no reason. Post it and go. School, work, family, burnout — all fine. LOA doesn't count against your activity or your standing.

The people who burn out are the ones who felt they couldn't step away. Don't be one.

docs.title: The short version
docs.text:
Ask questions. Nobody minds. Learn the radio format before anything else. Chase qualifications, not rank. Take care of your medic. Loud in the barracks, quiet in formation.

docs.title: [SERVER NAME] — 2LT and above
docs.text: Role guide 3 of 4 · Drawn from the Command Handbook and SOP

docs.title: The job
docs.text:
Command is a job, not a prize.

The rank means you're responsible for people — their training, their progression, their experience of this community, and whether they log in next week. It does not mean you've earned deference, better gear, or the right to win arguments.

The measure of a good officer here is not how well you perform in an operation. It is whether your people are still here in six months, and whether one of them is ready to take your job.

docs.title: The two rules you cannot break
docs.text:
1. The firewall. Command rank grants zero staff powers. You cannot ban, kick, mute, or warn anyone. Rule violations get reported to staff — you never handle them in character.

Where they overlap: a trooper who repeatedly RDMs is both a rule violation and a performance issue. Report it to staff and counsel them. Two tracks, both run.

2. Management doesn't command. No member of Management plays above Warrant Officer. If you're in Management, you're a Sergeant. This is structural and not waivable — the moment the owner sits at the top of the IC chain, every decision becomes unappealable and honest feedback stops.

docs.title: Running promotion boards
docs.text:
Required for every promotion to Sergeant and above.

Promoting to Board SGT / SSGT 3 members: 1 officer (chair), 1 SSGT+, 1 NCO from another battalion WO / 2LT / 1LT 3 members: 1 field grade (chair), 2 officers, 1+ external CPT and above 5 members: 1 High Command (chair), 3 officers, 1 external

At least one external member on every board. This is what stops battalions becoming closed loops that promote their own regardless of quality. Don't waive it.

Recuse yourself if you're close to the candidate. Same standard as staff.

docs.title: What you're scoring
docs.text:
Area Weight Knowledge — SOP, comms, ROE, chain of command 25% Leadership judgment — situational scenarios 35% Record — hours, quals, ops, counseling history 20% Peer and subordinate input 20%

Ask the people they lead. An officer beloved by the board and dreaded by their troopers is exactly the officer we must not promote. Solicit that input privately, and weight it.

docs.title: Deferral is the default for "close but not ready"
docs.text:
A deferral must come with specific written development items, a named mentor, and a re-board date — usually 30 days. Say out loud in the room that a deferral is not a failure. It changes how they hear it.

Written feedback within 48 hours, always — including on a pass.

docs.title: Discipline
docs.text:
Praise publicly. Correct privately. Always.

Step Action 1 Verbal counseling 2 Written counseling, with a specific improvement plan 3 Extra duty (max 3 sessions) 4 Qualification suspension 5 Reduction in rank — requires a board, appealable, trooper may bring an advocate 6 Removal from unit — requires High Command

docs.title: Hard rules
docs.text:
• No mass punishment. Banned outright.
  • No punishment while angry. Wait a session.
  • Every counseling names a behavior and a fix. "Do better" isn't counseling.
  • All command discipline is appealable — up the chain, or to the Ombudsman if the chain is the problem.
  • Records expire after 90 days clean.

docs.title: Insubordination — what it isn't
docs.text:
Refusing an unlawful order, asking a clarifying question, and raising a concern before executing are never insubordination.

Train your people to speak up. An officer who punishes dissent gets surrounded by silence, and silence is how operations fail.

docs.title: Running your unit
docs.text: Weekly minimums: one training session (hosted or delegated) · roster maintenance · one promotion candidate in development · 8 hours presence. Monthly: one operation written or led.

docs.title: Roster
docs.text:
Status Threshold Action Active 3+ hrs / 14 days — Low activity Under 3 hrs / 14 days Check-in message Inactive Under 1 hr / 21 days, no LOA Removal notice, 7 days to respond LOA Declared Held up to 60 days

LOA is free, unlimited, and needs no reason. People have jobs, school, and lives. A unit that punishes absence loses the people worth keeping.

docs.title: Succession — the thing you'll skip
docs.text:
Every command position must have a designated and trained second.

If you vanished tomorrow, would your unit function? If not, that's your failure to fix, this week.

  • Designate a 2IC when you take command
  • Your 2IC runs at least one training and one operation per month — designated-but-untrained is worthless
  • Handover on departure is written: roster state, ongoing issues, promotion pipeline, unit traditions

Term limits: battalion command is 4 months, renewable once. Stepping down at term end carries no stigma — most former commanders move into instructor or advisory roles, which are genuinely valuable and far less exhausting.

docs.title: Briefing an operation
docs.text:
The five-paragraph order. Five minutes. It's the difference between a coordinated op and forty people wandering.

  1. Situation — enemy, friendlies, what's happening
  2. Mission — one sentence: who, what, when, where, why
  3. Execution — your intent, scheme of maneuver, tasks by element
  4. Sustainment — ammo, medical, extraction
  5. Command & Signal — chain of command, nets, callsigns

Then run the AAR. Ten minutes, four questions: What was supposed to happen? What happened? What went well? What changes?

No rank in the AAR. A CT may tell you your plan was bad. An AAR where nobody criticizes anything is a wasted AAR — and if that's happening every week, it's a sign your people don't feel safe telling you things.

docs.title: Recognition
docs.text:
The most underused retention tool you have, and it's free.

Present awards in formation, out loud, with a specific reason. "For pulling two casualties out under fire at Sullust" beats a Discord ping every time.

Recognize the unglamorous. The trooper who ran the armory post reliably for three months has done more for this server than the one who got a lucky kill in an op. Build your award practice around that and watch what it does to your retention.

docs.title: Weekly checklist
docs.text:
1. Did I correct anyone publicly? (Don't.)
  2. Did anyone in my unit go a week without me speaking to them by name?
  3. Is my 2IC ready to run this without me?
  4. Who's closest to promotion, and what's specifically holding them back?
  5. Did I ask a subordinate for honest feedback and actually listen?
  6. Did anyone leave this month, and do I know why?
  7. Am I still having fun? If no, take an LOA before you burn out and take three people with you.

Full regulations: [DOCS URL] · Command Handbook · SOP §8

docs.title: [SERVER NAME] — Trial Moderator and above
docs.text: Role guide 4 of 4 · Drawn from the Staff Handbook and Charter

docs.title: The job — all of it
docs.text:
1. Keep players safe — harassment, hate, predatory behavior
  2. Keep the game fair — cheating, exploiting, griefing
  3. Keep the server running — technical issues, stuck players, broken props

That's the entire list. Staff don't run the roleplay, don't resolve in-character disputes, don't command troops, and don't use tools to shape the story.

If you took this for the powers, it will show inside a month.

docs.title: The firewall — read this twice
docs.text:
Staff authority grants zero in-character authority. Command authority grants zero staff powers.

  • A Superadmin playing a CT takes orders from a Sergeant and says "Yes, Sergeant."
  • A Marshal Commander cannot ban, kick, mute, or warn.
  • You may hold both — declare which hat you're wearing the moment it matters.
  • You may never use staff tools in a dispute you are personally part of. Call someone else. Every time. No exceptions.

Violating the firewall is Strike-and-review on the first occurrence. It's the fastest way off the team.

docs.title: Evidence — the hardest rule here
docs.text:
No evidence, no punishment. If the log has no evidence attached, the appeal is granted automatically.

No exceptions. Not for obvious cases, not for repeat offenders, not for Management.

Offense Required Chat Screenshot with timestamp and surrounding context Voice Audio clip, or 2+ independent witness statements Cheating Video clip, 30 seconds minimum, showing the behavior Exploiting Video showing the exploit in use RDM / griefing Video or damage logs + witness statement Harassment Screenshots of the pattern, not one message

Context is mandatory. One line without what preceded it is a fragment, not evidence. Clips show the behavior, not the aftermath. Collect witness statements separately — don't let them compare notes first.

Evidence gets attached at the time of punishment, not scrambled for later when someone appeals.

Uncertain means no punishment. An unjust warning damages that player's whole relationship with the server; a violation you let slide affects one incident. The asymmetry isn't close.

docs.title: Running a sit
docs.text:
1. Acknowledge the report. "On my way" or "Standby." Never leave one hanging.
  2. Gather evidence before you pull anyone — don't tip off a suspected cheater by teleporting them.
  3. Pull both parties.
  4. Reporter speaks first, uninterrupted.
  5. Reported speaks, uninterrupted.
  6. Ask clarifying questions. Don't lecture.
  7. Rule — state the rule, the finding, the punishment, plainly.
  8. Log it — rule, evidence, punishment, reasoning.
  9. Return both parties.

Do: stay calm regardless of tone · explain the rule, not just the penalty · tell them how to appeal · thank the reporter even when the report doesn't hold up.

Don't: argue · threaten extra punishment for arguing · discuss other players' punishments · make jokes at anyone's expense · rule on something you're unsure about.

docs.title: When you're being abused
docs.text:
You're not required to absorb it. Warn once — "I'm ending this sit if this continues" — then end it, apply the appropriate punishment for the conduct, log it, move on.

You do not have to win the argument. You are not required to make them agree with you.

docs.title: Escalate — don't guess
docs.text:
• The punishment exceeds your ban limit
  • It involves another staff member, Head of Staff, or Management
  • You're personally involved
  • Cheating suspected but evidence is ambiguous
  • Tier 4 or 5
  • The rule is unclear or the situation isn't covered
  • You're angry

That last one is real. "I'm too heated for this, can someone take it" is a completely acceptable sentence and nobody will think less of you.

docs.title: Recuse yourself when
docs.text:
You're a party to the incident · the player is in your battalion and it's battalion-related · they're a close friend or someone you have friction with · you issued the punishment being appealed · you stand to gain in character.

Recusal is free and expected. The cost of not recusing is that every ruling you ever make becomes suspect.

docs.title: The punishment matrix
docs.text:
Tier First Second Third 1 Minor Verbal warning (logged) Formal warning 1–3 day ban 2 Disruptive Formal warning 1–3 days 7 days 3 Serious 3–7 days 14–30 days Permanent 4 Severe 30 days Permanent — 5 Zero tolerance Permanent — —

Correction before punishment. A Tier 1 from a new member gets an explanation first — a rule nobody taught them is our failure, not their violation.

Adjust one tier either way with written justification. More than one needs Senior Admin approval.

Non-ban options exist and are usually better: voice mute, text mute, prop restriction, job restriction. Reach for these before a ban.

Tier 1 and 2 warnings expire after 90 days clean.

docs.title: Conduct
docs.text:
No tools for personal gain, entertainment, or IC advantage No spawning items for yourself or others outside approved events No noclip, godmode, or spectate outside an active sit No discussing active cases outside the staff channel No accepting anything of value connected to your duties Donation status is invisible in a sit — preferential treatment is immediate removal No retaliation against anyone who appealed or reported you — permanent bar Hold yourself to the Charter more strictly than anyone else, publicly

Two strikes. Strike one is documented and known to the staff team. Strike two is removal. Immediate removal for: firewall violation, punishing without evidence twice, retaliation, falsified evidence, Tier 4/5 conduct, or paid preferential treatment.

Staff have the same appeal rights as players. Removals can go to the Ombudsman.

docs.title: Take the LOA
docs.text:
Free, unlimited, no justification required. Post it in the staff channel and go. It doesn't count against activity or standing.

Burnout kills staff teams. Every single time. Take the LOA before you become the person snapping at players in sits.

docs.title: The standard
docs.text:
Every decision gets measured against one question:

Would this look defensible if it were posted publicly, with full context, tomorrow?

Yes → act. No → don't. Unsure → escalate.

That's the whole job.

docs.title: [SERVER NAME] — The persistent war
docs.text: v1 runs on a spreadsheet. Prove the loop is fun before anyone writes code.

docs.title: The idea
docs.text:
Operations aren't disposable. Every op is fought over a named system, the outcome persists, and what you hold changes what the ship can do next week.

Losing should be felt in the base, not announced in Discord. That's the whole design. A trooper who walks into a hangar with two fighters missing because we lost Sullust understands the campaign without reading a word.

docs.title: The map
docs.text:
12 systems in an Outer Rim theater. Original space — not canon planets fought over in canon battles, which keeps us free of lore arguments.

Each system has:

Field Name Original Control −5 (Separatist) to +5 (Republic), starts at 0 Adjacency 2–3 connected systems Trait One mechanical effect when held (see below)

Starting position: Republic holds 3, Separatists hold 3, 6 contested at 0. We start with a foothold, not a victory — there has to be somewhere to go in both directions.

docs.title: Control
docs.text: Value State +3 to +5 Republic held — trait active +1 to +2 Republic contested 0 Contested −1 to −2 Separatist contested −3 to −5 Separatist held — enemy trait active

docs.title: How it moves
docs.text:
Event Change Main operation won (Saturday) +2 Main operation lost −2 Minor operation won (Thursday) +1 Minor operation lost −1 Partial success +1 or −1, planner's call Weekly drift ±1 toward whoever holds the majority of adjacent systems

Weekly drift is what makes the map feel alive between ops. A system you took but can't support will slide back, and that's correct — it's how you teach that the map has a shape.

docs.title: Supply lines
docs.text:
A system is supplied if a chain of Republic-held systems connects it to our home station's system.

Unsupplied systems: trait inactive, drift doubles against us, and operations there start at a stated disadvantage in the brief.

This is the strategic layer. It means the map isn't a scoreboard — position matters, and High Command has an actual decision to make about where to fight next.

docs.title: System traits
docs.text:
Hold the system, get the effect. Lose it, lose the effect.

Trait Effect when held Shipyard Fighter losses replaced between ops Foundry Heavy weapons and explosives fully stocked in the armory Bacta source Medic supplies at full; faster revives Relay Long-range sensors extended; enemy ops telegraphed a week out Fuel depot Transport and armor available for ops Training world Sim deck scenario rotation expanded Listening post Reveals adjacent system control values Garrison Passive defense; drift resists one step

Enemy-held systems apply the inverse where it makes sense — an enemy Foundry means tougher droid compositions in that theater.

docs.title: What loss actually looks like
docs.text:
The point of the whole system. When we lose ground, the base changes, visibly, without announcement:

  • Fighters missing from the hangar rack. Physically absent.
  • Armory heavy weapons locker locked with a supply notice.
  • Medbay supply shortage — longer revive times.
  • Sensor board showing fewer systems.
  • A system marked lost on the bridge map.

Conversely, winning opens things: new battalions unlock at milestones, new maps enter the op rotation, new equipment reaches the armory.

docs.title: Battalion unlocks
docs.text:
Locked units don't exist yet in-fiction. They arrive as campaign events.

Unit Trigger 41st Elite Corps Hold a jungle-theater system at +3 91st Recon Three consecutive successful recon ops 327th Star Corps Hold 6 systems simultaneously Republic Commando Escalation trigger — 8 systems held

Opening a battalion is a server-wide event, not a Discord announcement. Do a ceremony. It's free and people remember it for a year.

docs.title: Running it — v1
docs.text:
A spreadsheet and a hand-updated map image. That's it.

Column System · Control · Adjacency · Trait · Supplied Y/N · Last op · Last changed

Weekly cycle, Sunday: 1. Apply operation results 2. Apply drift 3. Recompute supply lines 4. Update the map image 5. Post the change summary to Discord 6. Apply the base state — lock the armory, pull the fighters, whatever changed

Fifteen minutes a week. Owned by Naval command or a designated campaign officer.

Do not build this in Lua until it has run for two months on a spreadsheet. If the loop isn't fun by hand, code won't fix it — and if it is fun, you'll know exactly what to build.

docs.title: Design rules
docs.text:
Never let it snowball. If we hold 10 of 12, escalate enemy strength hard. A campaign that's already won is a campaign nobody shows up for.

Never let it collapse. Below 2 systems held, enemy drift stops. Losing is a story; being unable to fight back is people leaving.

The map serves the roleplay, not the reverse. If a system change would produce a great story, the campaign officer may adjust it. Publish the reasoning.

Publish every change. Control values, drift, supply state — all visible. A hidden campaign is indistinguishable from no campaign.

Give Naval a real job. They run the map, brief High Command, and recommend where to fight. It's the only thing that makes bridge duty meaningful.

docs.title: The point
docs.text:
"We lost Sullust three weeks ago and tonight we're taking it back."

That sentence fills a server, and no amount of standalone event content produces it.

v1 spreadsheet-only. Revisit for in-game implementation after two months of live operation.

docs.title: [SERVER NAME] — Build a decent operation in 45 minutes
docs.text: For the Event Planner corps · Templates, structure, and the rules that stop burnout

docs.title: Why this document exists
docs.text:
One person writing every operation is the single most common way a server dies. They produce brilliant work for three months, burn out, quit, and the server has no content pipeline. It's happened to hundreds of communities.

This playbook exists so an operation takes 45 minutes to build, not six hours, which is what makes a six-person planner corps possible instead of a one-person heroic effort.

docs.title: Corps rules
docs.text:
Rule Standard Minimum planners 6. Below 4, recruit before you schedule. Saturday main op lead Rotates weekly. Nobody runs two in a row. Ops per planner Maximum 2 per month Lead time Template picked 5 days out, brief written 2 days out Approval Thursday minor ops: none. Saturday main ops: one other planner reads it. LOA Free, unlimited, no reason required

If you're dreading writing it, hand it off. A traded op is normal. A resented op is visible to everyone playing it.

docs.title: The 45-minute build
docs.text:
Minutes Do 0–5 Pick a template. Pick a campaign system it's fought over. 5–15 Fill the five-paragraph order. 15–25 Place the map — spawns, objectives, enemy positions. 25–35 Set enemy composition and waves from the table below. 35–40 Write the two branch outcomes: what changes on a win, what changes on a loss. 40–45 Post the brief. Assign element leads.

Don't write a story. Write a situation and let the players make the story. Every hour you spend on narrative is an hour that produces less fun than an hour spent on the map.

docs.title: The five templates
docs.text: Every operation on this server is one of these five, reskinned. That is a feature.

docs.title: T1 — DEFENSE
docs.text:
Hold a position against escalating waves.

Best for: large turnouts, mixed skill levels, new players. Hardest to run badly. Structure: friendlies fortify → 3–5 waves of increasing pressure → final push → hold or fall back. Win: position held at timer. Watch for: waves that arrive from the same direction every time. Rotate the axis.

docs.title: T2 — ASSAULT
docs.text:
Take a defended objective.

Best for: coordinated groups, 20+ players, showcasing combined arms. Structure: insertion → advance under contact → breach → clear → hold against counterattack. Win: objective held for 5 minutes after clearing. Watch for: a single chokepoint turning it into a meat grinder. Always build two approaches.

docs.title: T3 — BOARDING
docs.text:
Fight through a hostile vessel, or repel boarders on our own.

Best for: medium turnouts, CQB, 104th and Coruscant Guard showcases. Structure: breach the airlock → clear compartments → reach the objective (bridge, reactor, prisoner) → extract. Win: objective secured, extraction with acceptable casualties. Watch for: corridors so tight that only the front two players get to shoot. Use parallel routes.

docs.title: T4 — ESCORT
docs.text:
Move something fragile from A to B.

Best for: armor and transport showcases, teaching coordination, medium turnouts. Structure: link up → move along a route → 2–3 ambushes → arrival. Win: the package survives. Watch for: the convoy outrunning its infantry. Build in forced halts.

docs.title: T5 — RECON
docs.text:
Find something without being found.

Best for: small turnouts (8–15), 91st showcases, weeknights, when you want something different. Structure: insert quietly → locate the objective → observe and report → exfiltrate, contact optional. Win: intelligence gathered and reported. Contact is a partial failure, not a fail. Watch for: players who want to shoot things. Brief the intent clearly or they'll turn it into T2.

docs.title: Enemy composition
docs.text:
Scale by turnout. These are starting points — adjust after your first run.

Turnout B1 B2 Droideka Commando Vehicle 8–15 25–40 4–6 1 2 0–1 15–25 40–70 8–12 2 3–4 1 25–40 70–120 15–20 3–4 5–6 2

Composition rules: - B1s are the volume. They should die easily and constantly. That's the fun. - B2s are pressure. They make players use cover. - Droidekas are events. One droideka should change the shape of a fight. Never spawn four at once. - Commando droids are threats. Use them to make players nervous, not to kill people. - Tactical droids are objectives. A named enemy commander gives the op a face.

Escalate in waves, not in one lump. Three waves of 20 beats one wave of 60 in every measurable way.

docs.title: The brief
docs.text:
Five-paragraph order, five minutes at muster. Never longer.

  1. Situation — enemy, friendlies, what's going on
  2. Mission — one sentence: who, what, when, where, why
  3. Execution — commander's intent, scheme of maneuver, tasks by element
  4. Sustainment — ammo, medical, extraction
  5. Command & Signal — chain of command, nets, callsigns

Give the ground commander the mission, then get out of the way. You built the situation. They fight it. Resist the urge to correct their plan mid-op because it isn't the one you imagined.

docs.title: Campaign integration
docs.text:
Every operation is fought over a named system on the campaign map, and you write both outcomes before you run it.

Example On a win Control of [system] +2. Supply line to [adjacent] opens. Armory restocks heavy weapons. On a loss Control −1. Enemy pressure on [adjacent] increases. Two fighters unavailable next week.

Write the loss branch honestly. An operation the players cannot lose has no stakes, and they can tell. Losing a system and having to take it back three weeks later produces better stories than winning every Saturday.

docs.title: Running it
docs.text:
Do Don't Set up the map before muster Build while players wait Announce the timer at the start Let it run 90 minutes because it's going well Let the ground commander command Rescript mid-op because they surprised you Adjust enemy spawns live if it's lopsided Add enemies because players are doing well Call ENDEX cleanly Let it fizzle out Run the AAR immediately Skip it because everyone's tired

Target duration: 60 minutes. 90 is the ceiling. Ending while people still want more is the correct feeling to leave them with.

docs.title: The AAR
docs.text:
Ten minutes. Four questions. No rank in the AAR — a CT may tell a Colonel the plan was bad, and may tell you the op was bad.

  1. What was supposed to happen?
  2. What actually happened?
  3. What went well?
  4. What do we change?

Log the answers. They feed the campaign map and the next planner's build.

docs.title: After the op — five minutes
docs.text:
Post to the planner channel:

Template used · System fought over · Turnout · Duration · Outcome and campaign effect · One thing that worked · One thing that didn't

That last pair is the whole library. Six planners each contributing two lines a month builds an institutional memory that no single person could hold, and it's what makes the seventh planner good on their first attempt.

docs.title: Burnout check
docs.text:
1. Am I building more than 2 ops a month?
  2. Have I led two Saturdays in a row?
  3. Am I dreading this one?
  4. Did I take a month off in the last six?

Any yes: hand it off or take the LOA. The corps exists so that's a normal move, not a failure.

Templates are starting points. Improve them and the improvement goes in the playbook.

docs.title: [SERVER NAME] — Boot camp, run cold off the page
docs.text: Instructor-facing · 15 minutes · Delivers the Basic Rifleman qualification

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
This is the fifteen minutes that decides whether this person comes back. Not the Saturday op, not the campaign — this. Treat it accordingly.

Duration 15 minutes. Hard stop. Class size 1–6. Above 6, run two sessions. Location Simulation deck, range configuration You need Range targets loaded, a spare rifle, a sponsor standing by Outcome Basic Rifleman qualification + assigned sponsor + assigned fire team

Nobody fails this course. Two attempts, then you work with them one-on-one until they pass. This is the one gate that never gates.

Say things in your own words. The scripted lines below are floor, not ceiling — they exist so you never have to think about what comes next.

docs.title: MINUTE 0–2 — Meet them
docs.text:
"Welcome aboard. I'm Sergeant [name], I'll be running you through basics. Fifteen minutes, then you're with your unit. What do I call you?"

They don't have a name yet — they're a CT with a number. Use the number. It's not an insult, it's the setup for the payoff later.

Do: get their name/number, ask if they've played GMod RP before, ask if they're on mic.

Don't: open with rules. Don't open with lore. Don't say "before we begin, read the Charter."

"You've got a number right now, not a name. You earn one. Usually your squad gives it to you and usually it's about something embarrassing. That's tradition, don't fight it."

If they're not on mic: that's fine, say so explicitly. "No mic is fine, plenty of people run text. You'll want one eventually for ops but nobody's going to hassle you."

docs.title: MINUTE 2–5 — Courtesies and chain of command
docs.text:
Keep this fast. It's the least fun part and they'll absorb it by doing, not by hearing.

Demonstrate, then have them do it:

  1. The salute. "Officers only — anyone Second Lieutenant and up. First time you see them each session."
  2. Reporting. "Sir, CT-2247 reporting as ordered." Have them say it out loud once.
  3. Acknowledging. "'Yes sir,' 'copy,' or 'wilco.' Not 'ok,' not 'yeah.'"

Then the one that actually matters:

"Bearing is situational. In formation, on an op, at your post, on the bridge — discipline. In the barracks, in the mess, off duty — be as loud as you want. Knowing which room you're in is the whole skill. Nobody here wants you standing at attention in the mess hall."

And this, explicitly:

"If you think an order is wrong, say so before you do it, then do it. 'Sir, recommend we go east instead.' That's not insubordination and nobody will punish you for it. If somebody does, report it — that's on them, not you."

Say that out loud even though it's in the guide. It's the single line that most changes how someone behaves in their first month.

docs.title: MINUTE 5–8 — Weapons handling
docs.text:
Hands on the rifle. Talking stops.

Demo Then they do it Draw and holster Both, twice Reload Once Weapons Cold — holstered Call it, they comply Weapons Tight — drawn, fire on positive ID Call it, they comply Weapons Free — fire at discretion Call it, they comply

"Cold is the base default on this ship. If you're walking around with a rifle out and nobody's called Amber, someone's going to say something."

Call the three states in random order and watch them respond. That's the assessment — takes thirty seconds and it sticks better than an explanation.

docs.title: MINUTE 8–11 — Comms
docs.text:
This is the highest-value block in the course. If you're running short on time, cut somewhere else.

Write it out or say it slowly, twice:

"[Them], this is [me], [message], over."

Have each of them transmit one call to you. Any content. Correct the format once, kindly, and move on.

Then the five words:

Over Done, respond Out Done, no response Copy / Roger Got it Wilco Got it, doing it Say again Repeat — never say "repeat"

Then the three that interrupt everything:

"Check fire. Man down. Contact. These three stop whatever else is happening on the net. If you hear 'check fire,' you stop shooting immediately — not after one more shot."

Have them say each of the three out loud once. Muscle memory for the mouth.

docs.title: MINUTE 11–14 — The range
docs.text:
Ten targets, close and medium. Six hits to pass.

Before they fire:

"Positive ID before you shoot. Check what's behind your target. If I call check fire, you stop instantly."

Call "check fire" once during the run, unannounced, mid-string. That's the real test. Someone who keeps shooting gets one correction and one retry — and now they'll never forget it.

Score it out loud. "Eight of ten, and you stopped on check fire. That's a pass."

If they miss the standard: run it again immediately. Don't make it a thing. "Range nerves, everyone gets them. Go again."

docs.title: MINUTE 14–15 — Hand off
docs.text:
This is the part everyone skips and it's the part that determines retention.

  1. Award the qualification out loud. "CT-2247, you're Basic Rifleman qualified. That's logged. Congratulations."
  2. Introduce the sponsor by name, in person. Not a Discord link. Not "someone will find you." A person, standing there.

    "This is Corporal [name]. He's your sponsor. Anything you're confused about for the next two weeks, ask him — that's literally his job and he gets credit for it."

  3. Sponsor walks them to their battalion physically.
  4. Name their fire team members. Three or four people, by name.
  5. Give them one concrete next goal:

    "Get ten hours of duty time and a second qualification and you'll make Specialist. Medic and Comms are the easiest to pick up and the most useful to your squad. Marksman's the most fun."

  6. Point at the card. "Everything from today is on the Trooper Card. Keep it open."

Then stop. Don't add more. They're full.

docs.title: Failure modes — the things that lose people
docs.text: Don't Why Run over 15 minutes The single most common killer. They came to play. Lecture on lore Nobody has ever stayed for a lore lecture Say "go read the rules in Discord" They won't, and now they think we're bureaucratic Leave them without a sponsor The highest-correlation predictor of them not returning Haze, test patience, or make them stand at attention as a filter Immediate command discipline matter. Also just wrong. Spawn them into an empty map with no marker Fix the spawn, not the trooper Be visibly bored They can tell. It tells them what this place is like.

docs.title: Instructor self-check
docs.text:
After each session:

  1. Did I finish inside 15 minutes?
  2. Did they physically meet their sponsor and fire team?
  3. Did they transmit at least one radio call themselves?
  4. Did they leave with one specific next goal?
  5. Did they talk at all? If they said nothing for fifteen minutes, I ran a lecture, not a course.

Delivers: Basic Rifleman (Qualification Syllabi §01) · Full regulations: [DOCS URL]

docs.title: [SERVER NAME] — Pairing every new trooper with a person
docs.text: One page · The highest-leverage retention mechanic we have, and it costs nothing but policy

docs.title: Why
docs.text:
People stay for people.

A new member who has one named person to ask questions of returns at a dramatically higher rate than one who has a Discord channel and a rulebook. That's the entire theory, and it's the reason this program is written down and rewarded rather than left to good intentions.

Every recruit gets a sponsor. Within their first session. Every time.

docs.title: Who can sponsor
docs.text:
Requirement Standard Rank Corporal or above Tenure 30 days on the server Record No active counseling Load Maximum 2 active sponsees at a time Availability Reasonably active during the recruit's play hours

Match on time zone and play hours before anything else. A great sponsor who is never online when the recruit is is worse than an average one who is.

docs.title: What a sponsor does
docs.text:
When Action First session Meet them at the end of boot camp, in person. Walk them to their battalion. Introduce their fire team by name. First session, before they log Get one contact point — Discord handle, so they exist to you outside the server. Second session Check in. This is the one everyone skips and it's the one that matters most. Week 1 Take them into one activity — a sim run, a patrol, a drill. Anything with other people in it. Week 2 Push them toward their second qualification. Sit their range run if you can. Week 3–4 Introduce them to someone outside their fire team. Widening the circle is what makes them stay past month one. End of week 4 Sponsorship formally ends. Say so, and say they can still ask you anything.

Total time cost: roughly 30 minutes a week for four weeks.

docs.title: What a sponsor is not
docs.text:
• Not their commander. You may not outrank them for long. Advice, not orders.
  • Not staff. Rule violations go to staff. If your sponsee is cheating, report it — sponsorship is not cover.
  • Not a trainer. Instructors certify. You point them at the course and make sure they show up.
  • Not permanent. Four weeks. Then they're just a friend, which is the point.

docs.title: Rewards
docs.text:
Reward Earned by Credits Per sponsee reaching Specialist Sponsor Ribbon 5 sponsees reaching Specialist Promotion credit Sponsorship counts toward NCO and officer promotion criteria

We pay for this because it's the work that keeps the server alive, and unpaid invisible work reliably stops happening. A promotion board should ask an NCO candidate how many people they've sponsored and how those people are doing.

docs.title: Tracking
docs.text:
One row per pairing. A spreadsheet is fine at launch; it moves into the personnel file system later.

Recruit · Sponsor · Start date · Second-session check-in (Y/N) · Second qual date · Still active at 30 days (Y/N)

The only metric that matters: 30-day retention rate for sponsored vs. unsponsored recruits. If a recruit ever goes unsponsored, that's an accidental control group — note it. Within two months you'll know exactly what this program is worth, in numbers.

docs.title: When it fails
docs.text:
Sponsor goes inactive: the battalion NCO reassigns within 48 hours. Don't wait for the recruit to notice they've been abandoned.

Bad match: either party can request a swap, no reason required, no hard feelings. Say this out loud when you assign, so neither of them feels stuck.

Recruit goes quiet: one message. "Hey, haven't seen you on — everything alright?" No pressure, no guilt, no second message. Some people just move on, and chasing them makes the server feel needy.

No sponsor available: an officer takes it personally until one frees up. A recruit without a sponsor is a hole in the process, not an acceptable outcome.

docs.title: The one-line version
docs.text:
Nobody's first session ends without them knowing one person's name.

Referenced by: Command Handbook §7, NCO Guide, Onboarding Script minute 14

docs.title: [SERVER NAME] — What Is and Is Not True Here
docs.text: Document 2 of 6 · Version 1.0 · Authority: Management + Lore Officer

docs.title: 0. Why This Document Exists
docs.text:
Lore arguments are the single most common recurring conflict in Star Wars roleplay communities, and they are almost always unwinnable — because both people are right, citing different sources.

This document ends that. It defines what is true on this server. Not what is true in Star Wars generally. If something isn't addressed here, §8 tells you how it gets decided.

Bring a source to a lore argument and the answer is: "What does the Canon Scope say?" If it says nothing, file a ruling request. Do not argue in Discord.

docs.title: 1. Era and Timeline
docs.text:
Setting: 21–20 BBY, the middle years of the Clone Wars.

Specifically: after Geonosis and the Battle of Kamino, after Phase II armor is in general issue, before Order 66. The Republic is winning on some fronts and losing on others. The war has been going long enough that veteran clones exist and long enough that the shine has worn off.

Where our story sits: the server operates its own front. We are not re-enacting Ryloth or Umbara beat for beat. Our campaign (see Concept Doc §7) is an original Outer Rim theater running parallel to canon events. This gives us narrative freedom without contradicting anything.

Order 66 does not happen. The timeline does not advance to it. If the community ever wants a server-wide finale, that is a Management decision made deliberately, not a plot twist an event planner drops on a Tuesday.

Real-world time does not map to in-universe time. One real month is not one in-universe month. Time passes as the campaign requires.

docs.title: 2. Source Hierarchy
docs.text:
When sources conflict, this is the order of authority:

  1. This document. Always wins.
  2. Star Wars: The Clone Wars (2008–2020 series). Our primary visual and tonal reference. If it's in the show, it's true here.
  3. The films (Episodes II and III).
  4. Current Disney canon — novels, comics, reference books.
  5. Legends / Expanded Universe — permitted as a source of flavor and detail, particularly for unit histories, equipment variants, and planets. Not binding.
  6. Community-created lore — our own campaign history, unit traditions, character backstories. Binding on us, invisible outside.

Our line, stated plainly: we are Legends-permissive. We draw freely from Legends when it makes for better roleplay, and we default to the show when there's a conflict. We are not canon purists and we are not running a Legends-only server. This is a deliberate choice; it is not up for debate.

Explicitly not sources: video game mechanics (Battlefront balance is not lore), fan films, other servers' rules, and "I saw it on a wiki once."

docs.title: 3.1 Active at Launch
docs.text: Unit Status Notes 501st Legion Active Line infantry. Blue markings. 212th Attack Battalion Active Combined arms, siege. Orange markings. 104th Battalion "Wolfpack" Active SAR, void ops, EVA. Grey/maroon markings. Coruscant Guard Active Military police, base security. Red markings. Deployed detachment. Republic Navy Active Bridge crew and pilots. Naval uniform, not armor. Jedi Order Active, capped See §5.

docs.title: 3.2 Locked — Unlockable via Campaign
docs.text:
Unit Unlock condition 41st Elite Corps Campaign milestone: secure a jungle/forest theater system 91st Mobile Reconnaissance Campaign milestone: three consecutive successful recon ops Republic Commando (Delta-class) Campaign milestone: late-war escalation trigger 327th Star Corps Campaign milestone: TBD Doom's Unit / 187th Reserved, may not be used

Locked units do not exist yet in-fiction. Do not roleplay membership in them, do not wear their markings, and do not petition for early access.

docs.title: 3.3 Not Present
docs.text: Not on this server, in any form: Death Watch, Mandalorian factions as playable, bounty hunters as playable, Imperial-era units, First Order, Sith beyond scripted event antagonists, and any unit not listed above.

docs.title: 4.1 The Progression
docs.text:
This is one of the most important pieces of roleplay design on the server. Individuality is earned.

Stage Designation How you get it Recruit / CT CT-#### (randomly assigned) Joining Named Trooper Chosen name, e.g. CT-2247 "Hatch" Complete Basic Rifleman + 10 hours duty time, or earn it in an operation Callsign Squad callsign, e.g. WOLF 3 Assignment to a fire team Personalized armor Custom paint/markings Rank of Corporal or above, or purchased cosmetic

Names must be earned in-character. The traditional route is that a squad gives you one, usually derived from something you did — good or embarrassing. Command may also grant one for performance. You cannot simply pick one on day one.

docs.title: 4.2 Naming Standards
docs.text:
Permitted: short nicknames, trade-derived names, incident-derived names, trait-derived names. Examples of the register we want: Hatch, Sparks, Crosswire, Ridge, Tally, Dust, Kettle, Nine.

Not permitted: real-world celebrity names, meme names, names from other franchises, offensive names, names identical to major canon characters (no second Rex, Cody, Fives, Echo, Wolffe, Hardcase, Jesse, Kix, Waxer, Boil).

Jedi and Naval use ordinary Star Wars-style names, not clone designations.

docs.title: 4.3 Reserved Characters
docs.text:
Named canon characters — Rex, Cody, Wolffe, Anakin, Obi-Wan, Ahsoka, etc. — are not playable. They may appear as staff-controlled NPCs in scripted events only, and only with Management approval.
